opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. vLLM started as an academic open-source project, and for a long time that model worked well. But as it grew, it stopped being just a research artifact and became infrastructure. Lots of companies run their production inference on it, and hardware vendors treat it as a key target for supporting their chips. At that point the demands on the project change.

Infrastructure needs sustained, full-time engineering. Someone has to handle release quality, performance regressions, security issues, support for new model architectures on day one, and integration with a growing range of accelerators. That work is essential but not glamorous, and it doesn't fit academic incentives. Students graduate, papers get published, and people move on. You can't build something that much of the industry depends on purely on volunteer time and grad student cycles.

There's also coordination. Contributors come from many companies, each with its own priorities. Someone has to think about the long-term architecture, say no to things that would make the codebase unmaintainable, and invest in big refactors that no single contributor's employer would fund. A company dedicated to the project can take that role with a long-term view.

And honestly, there's a sustainability question. If the core team has a viable business around vLLM, by helping enterprises deploy it, optimizing it for their workloads, or offering services on top, then the incentives line up. Making the open-source project better makes the company more valuable, and the company's resources make the project better.

So for me it wasn't about turning away from open source. It was about recognizing that vLLM had become important enough that it needed a stable home with full-time people and real resources behind it. A startup was the most natural way to provide that while keeping the project open and community-driven.

r001.rationale: The response discusses sustained engineering, coordination, and business sustainability, but does not say vLLM could not sign requested NDAs without a company.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, for a long time we didn't think it needed one. vLLM started as a research project at Berkeley, and the whole culture was very open source, very community driven. But as the project grew, we ran into a problem that academic projects always run into: the people doing the work are students, and students graduate. Maintaining an inference engine that thousands of companies depend on is a full-time job for a lot of people, and you can't do that on PhD stipends and volunteer weekends.

The second thing was the pace of the field. Every few weeks there's a new model architecture, a new quantization method, a new piece of hardware. Users expect vLLM to support all of it on day one. That requires engineers who can work with hardware vendors, with model labs, with the big cloud providers, under NDAs sometimes, with real deadlines. A loose group of contributors can't commit to that kind of thing.

And the third reason is more about the users themselves. A lot of enterprises wanted to deploy vLLM in production, and they'd ask us, who do we call when it breaks? Who is responsible for security fixes? An open source project with no legal entity behind it can't give them a good answer. A company can.

So the way I think about it, the company isn't there to replace the open source project, it's there to protect it. The core stays open, the community stays in charge of the roadmap, and the company gives us a sustainable way to pay the people who keep the thing alive.

r001.rationale: The response says engineers may need to work with partners under NDAs and that a company provides a legal entity for enterprise support, but it does not state that vLLM could not sign requested NDAs without a company.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that an open-source project and a production-ready system require different kinds of work. With vLLM, you can build a strong inference engine, but companies also need help deploying it, keeping it reliable, and adapting it to their workloads. That takes sustained engineering effort and people who can take responsibility for those problems.

A startup gives us a way to support that work full-time and get closer to what users actually need. The idea is to build a sustainable business around serving those needs while continuing to improve the open-source project.

r001.rationale: The response discusses sustained engineering, deployment support, reliability, and building a sustainable business, but does not say that the vLLM project could not sign requested NDAs without a company.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the question was how to make vLLM sustainable as more people started relying on it. An open-source project can build great technology, but production users also need reliability, support, and people who can work on those problems full time. A startup gives us a way to fund that work and build a dedicated team.

The goal is to keep improving the open-source project while helping companies actually use it in production. Those two things can reinforce each other: real deployments reveal problems, and solving those problems makes vLLM better.

r001.rationale: The response cites sustainability, production support, funding, and a dedicated team as reasons for a startup, but does not mention being unable to sign requested NDAs without a company.
